title: Food Truck Best Stretch
aka: Maximum Sum Subarray of Size K
story: You run a food truck and log each day's profit; rainy days and festival fees mean some entries are negative. A magazine wants your best run of exactly k days in a row: the highest total profit of any k consecutive days.
task: Write bestStretch(profits, k). Return the largest sum of any k consecutive entries of profits.
The answer can be negative if every stretch of k days lost money.

examples.explanation: Every 2-day stretch lost money: -70, -110, -100. The best is -70; starting your running best at 0 would wrongly give 0.

hints: In the first example, days 0 to 2 sum to 380. The next stretch is days 1 to 3. Which days do they share?
Neighbouring stretches share all but one day at each end. Moving one day right drops the oldest day and adds a new one.
So you never need to add up k numbers again: update the previous total with one subtraction and one addition.
Sum the first k days as your best so far. Then for each next day i, add profits[i], subtract profits[i - k], and keep the largest total.
bruteForce: For every starting day, add up the next k profits and keep the largest. That is about n × k additions, roughly 25 million for 10,000 days and k = 5,000, and almost all repeated: neighbouring stretches share k - 1 days.

walkthrough: Picture a frame k days wide on the log. Sliding it right lets one day in and pushes one day out, and every day in between stays, so the total changes by just those two days.
• First frame, days 0 to 2: 120 - 40 + 300 = 380. The best so far is 380.
• Add day 5 (150), drop day 2 (300): 180 + 150 - 300 = 30. The best stays 380.
Start best at the first frame's total, not 0, so an all-losing log still gives the right answer.
solution.timeWhy: The first frame takes k additions, and each later slide takes one addition and one subtraction.
solution.spaceWhy: The function stores only the running total and the best total.
solution.takeaway: For a fixed-size window, keep a running total and update it as the window slides: add what enters, subtract what leaves. The same idea works for running counts, averages and character tallies.
